## Dates

- Soviets cut road, rail and canal access to West Berlin: 24 June 1948, the day after the Deutsche Mark was introduced in the western sectors.
- First American supply flights: 26 June 1948. The Americans called it Operation Vittles, the British Operation Plainfare.
- Blockade lifted: 12 May 1949, one minute after midnight.
- Flights continued to build up stocks until 30 September 1949.

## The numbers

About 278,000 flights and 2.3 million tonnes of cargo. Roughly two thirds of it was coal, which surprises students who imagine planes full of bread. The early C-47s carried about 3 tonnes; the C-54 Skymaster carried about 10, and by the autumn it was the backbone of the operation.

The "Easter Parade", 15 to 16 April 1949: 1,398 flights and 12,941 tonnes in 24 hours, a plane landing roughly every minute. General William Tunner staged it to break the crews' routine and to prove a point to Moscow.

The cost: 101 deaths in accidents, including 39 British and 31 American airmen, and the rest German civilians.

## Three airfields, three sectors

- Tempelhof in the American sector, with apartment blocks right at the end of the runway.
- Gatow in the British sector.
- Tegel in the French sector, built from scratch between August and November 1948 by around 19,000 Berliners, many of them women, in about 90 days. Paid in hot meals and a small wage.

Three air corridors from the west, each 20 miles wide, set down in a 1945 agreement, which is why the Soviets could block the roads but not the air without shooting.

## Gail Halvorsen

The story every child remembers. Lieutenant Gail Halvorsen, a C-54 pilot from Utah, started dropping sweets tied to handkerchief parachutes to children watching at the Tempelhof fence in July 1948. He'd wiggle his wings on approach so they knew it was him: "Uncle Wiggly Wings". The Berliners called the planes Rosinenbomber, raisin bombers. By the end around 23 tonnes of candy went down. He died on 16 February 2022, aged 101.

## Black Friday, 13 August 1948

Low cloud and rain over Tempelhof, one plane crashed off the end of the runway, another burst its tyres, and the rest stacked up overhead. Tunner, circling himself, ordered everyone home. After that: strict instrument rules, one attempt at landing, and if you missed you flew back to base with your load. This is my favourite bit for showing that logistics wins wars.

## Visiting, April 2023

Easter holidays, 3 April 2023. The memorial on Platz der Luftbrücke, unveiled 1951, that Berliners call the Hungerharke, the hunger rake: three prongs for the three air corridors. Did the Tempelhof building tour (€18, 2 hours). The old airfield is now Tempelhofer Feld, a park where people cycle down the runways. I stood where the children stood at the fence.

Packed light for that trip and regretted it, Berlin in April was 4°C ([[Packing list carry-on]]).

## Teaching it

Leaving Cert, "The Cold War" documents question. Daniel Harrington, *Berlin on the Brink: The Blockade, the Airlift, and the Early Cold War* (2012), p. 187: the airlift was not expected to succeed through the winter, and Clay himself had doubts in October 1948. Good for the "was it inevitable?" question.

Pair this with [[Mauerfall 1989]] to bracket the whole divided-city story, forty years from the blockade to the night the crossings opened. A colleague's note [[Projektstatus Berlin]] reminded me that the old Tempelhof terminal is now offices and event space.
